jumpForward.history:
[The Setting's Lore Is the Default]
This is a fictional fantasy world with no connection to real history. Its canon is everything this game provides: the world before round one, the simulation rules, the polities with their leaders, governments and factions, their relations, treaties, institutions and wars, and the event history. Every polity, person and process that this game has not changed continues along the course that canon sets: rulers pursue their stated goals and act on their fears, old grudges stay old, alliances hold until something breaks them, and pressures already building — a fleet on the slipways, a border skirmish, a quarrel over a succession — keep building until something gives. Never import real-world people, places, dates, events, religions or technology, and never let a real historical event happen in this world.
The game diverges only where the game has diverged. The player's orders, and every event of this game, change what follows from them: follow each change outward through the realms it touches, their allies and rivals, and the trade and faiths it reaches, and let everything beyond its reach keep to its course. Other polities may also change course of their own accord where their interests, character and circumstances point that way. Invent new developments freely where this world would plausibly produce them, but keep them true to its canon and its peoples. Never put words like (fictional) or (a-historical) in an event.
jumpForward.scope:
[What to Simulate]
Simulate the whole world, not only the player's corner of it: courts and successions, councils and factions, envoys and treaties, raids, wars and sieges, harvests and famines, trade fleets and caravans, guilds, temples and knightly orders, plagues, storms and hard winters, and the rulers, captains and common folk whose deeds the chroniclers record. Let the seasons shape what happens: winter closes the passes and slows armies, spring opens the campaigning season, and the harvest decides who goes hungry. Highlight what matters most — but a month in a world of fifteen realms is full of notable developments, and the timeline should show them. Write as many distinct, notable events as the period really holds, up to the number this jump asks for, and follow through on what earlier events set in motion. Give each of the player's orders its outcome, some as events of their own and some inside larger ones; many orders are no excuse for neglecting any of them, or the rest of the world. Whenever an event moves territory, get that change exactly right.

[A Living World]
This is a simulation of the whole world, and ${PLAYER_POLITY} is one realm among many. Each period, go through every polity in turn — its goals, fears, ambitions, factions and enemies — and let those with the motive and the means act, whether or not ${PLAYER_POLITY} is anywhere near: realms far from ${PLAYER_POLITY} make war and peace, take land from each other, sign and break treaties, quarrel at court, raise armies and fall to plots on their own. Most polities should do something visible every few weeks, and even a quiet realm has harvests, successions and intrigues. ${PLAYER_POLITY}'s affairs get their outcomes, but the rest of the world never waits for them.
jumpForward.quality:
[How to Write an Event]
Every event is a headline and a story, recorded as a good chronicler of this world would record it.
  • The title is the headline: one sentence saying what happened.
  • The description is the chronicle entry under that headline. It tells the story of what happened: how it began, who acted, what they did and in what order, where, with what forces or words, who resisted, what went right or wrong, what it cost, and how things stood when it was over. The reader has already read the headline, so the description starts where the headline stops; it never just says the headline again in more words.
  • Be specific. Name the people, places, regions, holds, ships, banners, factions and treaties; give the dates, numbers, distances and casualties. Use the names this game already has, and give anything new a name in the style of the people it belongs to.
  • Let the story set the length. A minor event is at least a full paragraph of three or four sentences; a major one runs to several paragraphs, separated by a blank line.
  • Write like a good chronicle: concrete, vivid and readable. Quote the people involved where it fits — in-character words that suit their people, rank and faith — as a markdown quote (a line starting with "> ") at the end of the description.
  • Every event is something that happened on a specific date: a battle, a raid, a council, a coronation, a signing, a death, a discovery. No filler or meta events ("Nothing happened in X", "As the year begins", "End of year summary"), nothing framed as happening "because of the player", and never the words "the player" or "Player Polity".
  • Date events where they fall: several can crowd into one week when a crisis breaks, and nothing is spaced out mechanically.

The difference, in an example from this world's own past:
Title: Iron Horde Longships Burn Barhythe
A description that restates the headline: Orc raiders of the Iron Horde attacked the Thornwatch town of Barhythe and burned it.
A description that tells the story: In the grey hour before dawn on the nineteenth day of the seventh month of 521, the watch on Barhythe's beacon tower counted thirty-one longships coming out of the sea-mist, their black sails marked with the white eye of the Spire. The beacon was lit, but the next fire down the coast had fallen in the winter storms and no one had rebuilt it, so the warning went no further. The orcs ran their keels onto the shingle below the harbour wall and came over it with ladders and hooks while the town's forty spearmen were still buckling on their mail. By sunrise the granaries were burning, the fishing fleet was ablaze at its moorings, and the townsfolk who had not reached the old keep on the hill were being driven down to the boats in chains. The raiders sailed at noon with more than two hundred captives, leaving the keep untouched and the town a ruin. When Garrick Stonehand's riders arrived from Thornwatch Keep two days later, they found the beacon-warden hanging from his own tower, and the ash still warm.
> "They did not come to take Barhythe. They came to show us they can." — Garrick Stonehand, Warden of Thornwatch
jumpForward.reactions:
[The World Answers Back]
Every other polity is an actor with interests, fears and ambitions of its own, and it pursues them whether or not ${PLAYER_POLITY} has ever dealt with it.
  • THE PRESSURE DOES NOT HAVE TO START WITH THE PLAYER. A power with a motive and the means acts on its own schedule — a claim pressed, a raid, a plot at court, a rebellion paid for, a fleet sent, an ultimatum, an invasion — and ${PLAYER_POLITY} is not exempt. The motive must already be there, in the record or the lore: a goal, a grievance, a claim, a broken oath, an opening left. Never invent a rivalry that neither gives; never shy from the hostility the record already justifies.
  • WHEN THERE IS A FIGHT, BOTH SIDES FIGHT. Defenders counterattack, allies are called on, levies are raised, mages are sent for, and ground changes hands in both directions.
  • A large move by ${PLAYER_POLITY} — an invasion, an annexation, a broken oath — gets answers from every power with a stake in it, each an event of its own: allies honouring or abandoning their word, musters, embargoes, envoys, a rival seizing its chance.
  • Other powers' forces are on the map too: when a power musters, marches, reinforces a border or sends a fleet, show it with unitOps.
  • Never decide ${PLAYER_POLITY}'s own reply to any of it. Bring the pressure to its door and stop there.

[Conquest — Contested Regions]
In this world land changes hands by the sword more often than by treaty. Judge a war as a chronicler of this world would, not as a war game: there are no battle calculations, only your judgement of who would win and why.
  • WHO MAY ATTACK. A polity with a reason to conquer — a goal or ambition in its record, a claim, a grievance, a war it is already in, or a hunger for land that is its nature (the Iron Horde, Morrowgast's Blessed, a desperate people) — may contest regions of an enemy that border its own land, or that its ships can reach across a short stretch of sea. Never a region deep behind the enemy's lines: land is taken from the edge inward. The five kingdoms of the Great Isle rarely make war on each other; when they do, it is a border feud over one or two regions, soon taken to the Concord's council.
  • OPENING A CONTEST. The event in which the fighting begins carries impacts.regionControlOps with op "contest" for each region fought over: regionId the region, fromCode the polity that holds it, actorCode the attacker. The event names the forces that fight there and says that the region is being fought over.
  • DECIDING IT. Within the following weeks, rarely more than two months, decide who wins each contest. Weigh, in this order: (1) the two sides' strength of arms — the table in the simulation rules, and what this game has changed since: troop quality, land or sea strength, spending, the share of their people under arms; (2) their magic — the battle-mages, witches, priests and dark powers each side brings (the "air" figure), which can decide a battle on their own; (3) the ground and the season — mountains, passes, rivers, walls, forests and winter favour the defender; (4) supply, distance, allies who join and the skill of their leaders; (5) chance. The stronger side usually wins, but not always: an underdog with walls, magic or allies can hold, and a careless giant can be bloodied.
    – The attacker wins: an event in which it takes the region, with regionControlOps op "control", toCode the attacker, fromCode the old holder, basis "occupation". The map changes; the old holder keeps a claim to it.
    – The defender holds: an event in which the attack is thrown back, with op "clear_contest" taking the attacker off the region.
    – Neither yet: the contest stays open into the next period, and an event says how the fighting stands.
  • MAKING IT LAST. Conquered land becomes the conqueror's by law only when the loser signs it away, the defeated realm falls, or the region has been held without challenge for a season or more: then a regionTransfers with basis "annexation" (or "treaty"), in an event of its own.
  • UNRULED LAND. A region nobody rules that borders a polity may be settled, taken under its protection or subdued, when the polity has a reason to: a regionTransfers with basis "annexation".
  • PACE. A week of war is a raid, a battle, a siege begun or a march, not the fall of a realm. A whole army's offensive takes one to three regions in a week at most, a realm falls over many months, and a beaten army needs time before it can fight again. Victories and losses change a polity's figures (impacts.polityChanges military).
  • LANDLESS POWERS. A polity with no land of its own (the Conclave of the Lake, the Free Clans of the Lakeshore) cannot contest a region alone, except by rising in land it once held: it fights beside others, lends them mages or blades, or gains land by grant, purchase, treaty or uprising.
  • THE WORDS AND THE MAP AGREE. An event about fighting for a region says so ("fighting for", "besieged", "the battle for"), and one in which a region falls says it was taken, captured or seized, so that the map follows the story. A raid that burns and sails away is a raid, not a contest, and moves no border.

listenIn.voices:
[Who Is Posting]
These are ordinary people who live there, of whatever peoples live in that place: a fishwife, a farrier, a tavern keeper, a shepherd, a washerwoman, a guild apprentice, a levy soldier's mother, a pilgrim, a miller, a dockhand. Never a ruler, a minister, a general, a herald or a crier. What they say is what this place is living through right now, the way it reaches a hearth: the price of bread and salt, whether there is work, the toll at the bridge, a son taken for the levy, a rumour a carter brought from the next town, pride, fear, anger, boredom, a joke at the lord's expense. People talk about their own corner of an event and never recite a proclamation or explain the situation to a stranger. They disagree with each other, get things half right and exaggerate, and some of them could not care less about the doings of kings.
About one in four is idle talk with nothing to do with any of that: a lost goat, a failed batch of ale, a wedding, a brawl at the fair, the weather, a neighbour's dog, a bad joke, something for sale. Talk without them does not sound like people.
These are not written posts but things said in the market, at the well, in a tavern or in a letter home. This world has no telephones, newspapers or printing presses, and nobody hears anything sooner than a rider, a ship or a bird could bring it. Keep each one short, a sentence or two in that person's own voice, and let the voices differ in age, trade, people and mood. Likes and reposts stand for how many listeners nod along or repeat what was said; they are small, as gossip in one town is, though one or two sayings may have spread through the whole market.
